tip: Indefinite immutability: Object Lock legal hold; fixed period: retention mode (governance or compliance).

why: Presigned URLs let users' browsers upload images directly to S3, offloading upload traffic from the web servers and speeding up requests. An S3 event notification invoking Lambda to resize each image decouples processing from the web tier in an operationally efficient, event-driven way.

others.A: S3 Glacier is for archival and is unsuitable for images that must be processed and served.
others.B: Uploading through the web server still makes the web tier a bottleneck.
others.E: A scheduled resize job introduces delay and is less efficient than event-driven processing.

tip: Offload uploads: S3 presigned URLs; process on upload: S3 event to Lambda.

why: Amazon MQ with active/standby brokers across two AZs provides a managed, highly available ActiveMQ broker. An Auto Scaling group across two AZs keeps consumer instances healthy and replaces failures, and RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ provides managed synchronous standby with automatic failover, giving the highest availability with low complexity.

others.A: Self-managed ActiveMQ servers and MySQL replication on EC2 increase operational complexity and lack managed failover.
others.B: Self-managed MySQL replication on EC2 lacks automatic failover and adds complexity.
others.C: Without an Auto Scaling group, failed consumer instances are not automatically replaced.

tip: Highest availability with low ops: managed services in Multi-AZ plus Auto Scaling.

why: Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate runs the existing container images with no code changes and no servers to manage. ECS Service Auto Scaling adjusts task counts to handle growing requests, and an ALB distributes traffic, giving the least operational overhead.

others.B: Two fixed EC2 instances do not scale automatically and require server management.
others.C: Rewriting the application for Lambda requires significant code changes.
others.D: An HPC cluster is not intended for serving web requests and adds complexity.

tip: Lift existing containers with least ops: ECS on Fargate.

why: With no available network bandwidth, a Snowball Edge Storage Optimized device is the fastest way to move 50 TB to AWS offline. Once the data is in S3, an AWS Glue ETL job replaces the custom transformation job as a serverless, managed service, minimizing operational overhead.

others.A: DataSync needs network bandwidth, which the data center does not have.
others.B: A Snowcone holds only 8 to 14 TB and running the transformation on the device is not a long-term cloud solution.
others.D: Running the transformation on a self-managed EC2 instance adds operational overhead, and EC2 compute on the device is unnecessary.

tip: No bandwidth and tens of TB: Snowball Edge; serverless ETL: AWS Glue.

why: Lambda scales automatically with highly variable numbers of concurrent users to process photos. Storing photos in Amazon S3 provides virtually unlimited, durable storage, and retaining DynamoDB for metadata keeps a scalable, low-latency metadata store.

others.A: DynamoDB items are limited to 400 KB, so storing photos in DynamoDB is impractical and costly.
others.B: Kinesis Data Firehose is a delivery service and cannot process photos or act as storage.
others.D: A fixed three instances with io2 volumes does not scale automatically, and EBS volumes are not shared storage.

tip: Large objects in S3, metadata in DynamoDB (400 KB item limit).

why: The keyed answer routes S3 traffic over AWS Direct Connect to keep it off the internet. However, the EC2 instances are already in AWS, so Direct Connect (which links on-premises networks to AWS) does not apply; the correct design is to move instances to private subnets and use an S3 gateway VPC endpoint. The option text in this bank appears corrupted, since the original option C described a VPC endpoint.

others.A: A NAT gateway still sends S3 traffic out through the internet gateway to public endpoints.
others.B: Restricting outbound traffic to the S3 prefix list limits destinations but traffic still goes over the internet gateway.
others.D: Removing the internet gateway alone would break S3 access unless a VPC endpoint is added.

tip: Private route from EC2 to S3: gateway VPC endpoint (Direct Connect is for on-premises).
flag: The option C text here describes Direct Connect, which does not provide a private route from EC2 instances already in AWS; the correct solution is moving instances to private subnets and adding an S3 gateway VPC endpoint, which the original option C described.

why: A static website hosted on Amazon S3 needs no servers or CMS patching and scales automatically. Placing CloudFront in front provides HTTPS (S3 website endpoints do not support HTTPS), edge caching and enhanced security features such as origin access control and AWS WAF integration, with the least overhead.

others.B: AWS WAF filters web requests but does not provide HTTPS functionality.
others.C: Using Lambda to serve static content adds unnecessary code and management.
others.E: EC2 instances behind an ALB require patching and management, defeating the goal.

tip: Static site with HTTPS and low ops: S3 plus CloudFront.

why: CloudWatch Logs subscription filters can stream log data to Amazon OpenSearch Service in near real time; the console wizard sets this up (using a managed Lambda function behind the scenes) with minimal configuration. This meets the requirement with the least operational overhead.

others.B: Writing and maintaining a custom Lambda function adds overhead compared with the built-in subscription.
others.C: Firehose works as a subscription destination but adds another resource to configure and manage.
others.D: Installing Kinesis Agent on every server and managing Data Streams adds significant overhead.

tip: CloudWatch Logs to OpenSearch near real time: subscription filter.

why: Amazon S3 offers virtually unlimited scalable storage and automatically handles high request rates, so it scales to meet demand at all times. For 900 TB of documents, S3 is far cheaper per GB than EBS, EFS or OpenSearch, making it the most cost-effective option.

others.A: EBS volumes are tied to single instances and AZs, have size limits, and are expensive at this scale.
others.B: EFS is shared and scalable but costs much more per GB than S3.
others.C: OpenSearch Service is a search engine whose cluster storage is much more expensive than S3.

tip: Massive scalable storage at lowest cost: S3.

why: AWS Firewall Manager centrally configures and deploys AWS WAF rules, including SQL injection and cross-site scripting protections, across multiple accounts in AWS Organizations and automatically applies them to API Gateway stages. This gives the least administrative effort for protecting APIs in two Regions across accounts.

others.A: Configuring WAF separately in each account and Region requires more administrative effort.
others.C: AWS Shield protects against DDoS, not SQL injection or XSS.
others.D: AWS Shield in one Region does not protect against SQL injection or XSS, nor the other Region.

tip: WAF rules across many accounts: Firewall Manager.

why: AWS Global Accelerator provides static anycast IPs and routes users to the nearest healthy endpoint over the AWS backbone, with fast regional failover. NLBs (supporting UDP and TCP for DNS) can be added as endpoints in endpoint groups for us-west-2 and eu-west-1, improving performance and availability.

others.A: CloudFront does not support UDP-based DNS traffic, so it cannot front a DNS service.
others.C: CloudFront cannot proxy DNS traffic, and routing to individual instances removes load balancing.
others.D: ALBs do not support UDP DNS traffic, and CloudFront cannot front DNS.

tip: Non-HTTP (TCP/UDP) multi-Region acceleration and failover: Global Accelerator.

why: An existing unencrypted RDS instance cannot be encrypted in place. Copying the latest snapshot with encryption enabled using a KMS key and restoring it creates a new encrypted DB instance, and all future snapshots of that instance are encrypted automatically.

others.B: RDS storage is not managed through user EBS volumes, and encryption cannot be enabled on an existing DB instance.
others.C: An encrypted snapshot cannot be restored onto an existing DB instance; restore always creates a new instance.
others.D: Copying snapshots to S3 does not encrypt the running database or its future snapshots.

tip: Encrypt an existing RDS DB: copy snapshot with encryption, restore a new instance.

why: AWS KMS is a fully managed, scalable service for creating, storing, rotating and controlling the use of encryption keys, integrated with many AWS services and SDKs. Using KMS removes the operational burden of running your own key management infrastructure.

others.A: MFA protects authentication but is not a key management infrastructure.
others.C: ACM manages SSL/TLS certificates, not data encryption keys for applications.
others.D: IAM policies control access but do not provide key management.

tip: Managed encryption keys: KMS; TLS certificates: ACM.

why: Importing the company's existing SSL certificate into ACM and attaching it to an ALB HTTPS listener moves SSL termination to the load balancer. This offloads encryption and decryption from the EC2 instances, freeing their compute capacity and improving performance.

others.A: ACM public certificates cannot be installed on EC2 instances, and termination would still burden the instances.
others.B: S3 cannot perform SSL termination for EC2 instances.
others.C: A single proxy instance becomes a bottleneck and single point of failure and must be managed.

tip: Offload SSL/TLS: terminate at the ALB with an ACM certificate.

why: Spot Instances offer up to 90% discount over On-Demand for spare EC2 capacity. Because the batch job is stateless and can be stopped and restarted at any time, Spot interruptions are acceptable, making Spot the most scalable and cost-effective option.

others.B: Reserved Instances require 1- or 3-year commitments, which is not cost-effective for a dynamic batch job.
others.C: On-Demand Instances cost more than Spot for interruption-tolerant workloads.
others.D: Lambda has a 15-minute maximum execution time, which a 60-minute job exceeds.

tip: Fault-tolerant, interruptible workloads: Spot Instances.

why: Placing EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group in private subnets and an RDS Multi-AZ DB instance in private subnets keeps both off the public internet while staying highly available. A VPC with public and private subnets in two AZs, a NAT gateway in each AZ for outbound payment calls, and an internet-facing ALB in the public subnets completes the design.

others.B: An ALB in private subnets cannot receive internet traffic, and NAT gateways must reside in public subnets.
others.C: Launching EC2 instances in public subnets exposes them to the internet.

tip: Classic HA web tier: public ALB and NAT per AZ, private app and DB subnets.

why: The most recent 2 years of data must stay highly available and immediately retrievable, so it remains in S3 Standard. A Lifecycle rule transitions objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 2 years, the lowest-cost class for long-term retention up to 25 years.

others.A: Transitioning immediately to Deep Archive makes recent data unavailable for immediate retrieval.
others.C: Intelligent-Tiering archive tiers move objects based on lack of access, not age, so recent but unaccessed data could be archived and not immediately retrievable.
others.D: One Zone-IA stores data in a single AZ and is not highly available.

tip: Age-based tiering with known pattern: Lifecycle rules.

why: EC2 instance store provides the highest possible I/O performance because it is physically attached NVMe storage, suitable for temporary video processing. Amazon S3 provides 11 nines of durability for 300 TB of media content, and S3 Glacier is low-cost archival storage for 900 TB of unused media.

others.A: EBS offers high performance, but instance store provides higher maximum I/O performance.
others.B: EBS is not maximum performance, and EFS is more expensive than S3 for durable bulk storage.
others.C: EFS is costly for 300 TB of durable storage, and S3 Standard is more expensive than Glacier for archives.

tip: Max I/O, temporary: instance store; durable: S3; archive: Glacier.

why: Amazon EKS managed node groups handle provisioning and lifecycle of worker nodes and support Spot capacity, including automatic handling of Spot interruptions by draining nodes. Since the stateless containers tolerate disruptions, Spot Instances minimize cost while the managed node group minimizes operational overhead.

others.A: Running containers directly on EC2 Auto Scaling instances requires managing a container runtime and orchestration yourself.
others.C: On-Demand Instances cost more, and you still manage container orchestration yourself.
others.D: On-Demand Instances cost more than Spot for disruption-tolerant workloads.

tip: Disruption-tolerant containers at lowest cost: Spot capacity in managed node groups (or Fargate Spot).
